title: Friends of one another
hookLine: believing men and women are protectors of one another (9:71)
last: SMALL, BRAVE, ORDINARY THINGS IN THE DARK.

cards: Start with grammar. An Arabic plural like "the believers" can cover a mixed group, the way "you all" does. But in some places the Qur'an says it twice: men and women, believing men and believing women.
At-Tawbah does it in verse seventy-one, right after a passage about the hypocrites, men and women, who egg each other on toward wrong.
Then the surah turns and describes the other kind of community, and gives it a word: awliya'. Friends. Allies.
People who stand at each other's side.

teach.b: Pickthall translates the verse's opening this way: "And the believers, men and women, are protecting friends one of another; they enjoin the right and forbid the wrong".
It goes on: they keep up the prayer, they pay the zakat, they obey God and His messenger, and God will have mercy on them. Awliya' is the plural of wali.
Its root, w-l-y, carries the sense of being near, close enough to turn toward. So a wali is a friend, but also an ally, a guardian, someone who has your back.
The same word can describe God's closeness to believers, and in another verse, a guardian in a family. Here it runs sideways, between people. And look at the list.
Men and women share every verb: both encourage good, both push back on wrong, both pray, both give. The verse doesn't divide the work and hand half to each. Why name both at all?
A report in Ahmad's Musnad gives one answer.

teach.h: UMM SALAMA ASKS; TEN PAIRS COME.
teach.b: Umm Salama, a wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, asked him: why are men mentioned in the Qur'an, and we are not? Later, she heard him reciting from the pulpit a new verse, in Surah al-Ahzab.
It names ten qualities, each one twice: Muslim men and Muslim women, believing men and believing women, truthful men and women, patient, giving, fasting, men and women who remember God much.

For all of them, forgiveness and a great reward. A woman asked a question, and the answer came back spelled out ten times over. Scholars disagree about many details of how men and women work together.
This verse is a common starting point: protectors of each other.

how: Muslims cite 9:71 when speaking of shared responsibility between men and women in faith and community life; how that cooperation is arranged in mosques, schools and families varies between scholars and communities.

o: rivals competing for the same prize
strangers kept at a careful distance
friends and allies at each other's side

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: the root: near, at your side
hypocrites who egg each other on

s: in 9:71, men and women share the same list of duties
both enjoin the right, forbid the wrong, pray and give zakat.
wali only ever means a saint
it means friend, ally, guardian, protector: someone near. here it runs between believers.
the verse in al-Ahzab names ten qualities for men and women
Muslim, believing, truthful, patient, giving, fasting, remembering God: each named for both.

games.q: you're Umm Salama. you ask the Prophet why the Qur'an mentions men and not women. what happens next, in the report?
o: he says women are included in the word for men.
a verse comes naming men and women, ten times over.
he says the question shouldn't be asked.
games.why: later she heard him recite 33:35 from the pulpit, naming every quality twice: for men and for women.

practice: Think of someone of the other sex in your life: a sister, a brother, a colleague, a classmate, a neighbor. Is there a place where their good idea went unheard, or their work was credited to someone else?
Picture standing at their side, speaking up for the right thing, simply and decently; if you pray, ask for that person by name.

wordCard.voice: Awliya'. Friends, allies, protectors, from a root that means to be near. Believing men and women, at each other's side. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: friends, allies, protectors; plural of wali, from the root w-l-y, to be near.

carryVoice: Your line: protectors of each other. The same verbs for both. Day four hundred twenty-three, counted.
